lang.thema: Claude Code with MCP: setup step by step, and what the pricing page lists
lang.titel: CLAUDE CODE + MCP: SETUP AND WHAT IT COSTS
lang.text:
You're pasting the same data into chat again. That copy-paste loop is a nightmare, and Claude Code with MCP exists to end it.

But the pricing page has the last word on cost. By the end, you'll know the setup steps and what the Free and Pro columns list. You'll see each page's own wording.

Start with the Free column. It says: Limited usage every 5 hours and every week. It also lists Chat on web, desktop, and mobile, and Search the web, create files, and run code.

Claude Code's overview page adds a condition. Most surfaces require a Claude subscription or Anthropic Console account. The Desktop app section says a paid subscription is required.

Step one is the install command on that overview page. Windows PowerShell and CMD each get their own line.

The page says the install command shows no progress while it downloads. So silence is normal. Riveting, I know. Then open a new terminal window and run claude --version. A working installation prints a version number.

Before step two, be sure to like, share and save this video.

If your shell says claude isn't found, the page points to Fix your PATH. Then start Claude Code in any project, and it prompts you to log in on first use. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set and you approve the key, Claude Code skips the login prompt.

If you see irm is not recognized, you're in CMD, not PowerShell. Git for Windows is recommended on native Windows so Claude Code can use the Bash tool.

The page says native installations automatically update in the background. Homebrew and WinGet installs do not auto-update; run brew upgrade or winget upgrade.

Not a terminal person? The same page lists a VS Code extension, a Desktop app with a Code tab, and a browser version.

The overview page's example prompt: write tests for the auth module, run them, and fix any failures. That's the documented example, not our run.

Now for MCP. The MCP page calls it an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. That open-source label describes the standard. It doesn't set what Claude costs, and the pricing page does that.

The MCP intro page says Claude, ChatGPT, Visual Studio Code, and Cursor all support MCP. Yes, even ChatGPT made the list. Its examples include Claude Code generating a web app from a Figma design.

The page says to connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat. Once connected, Claude can read and act on that system directly instead of working from what you paste. If you're connecting your first server, the page says start with the MCP quickstart.

Option 1 is Add a remote HTTP server. The command reads: claude mcp add, dash dash transport http, then a name, then a URL.

The page's real example connects Notion.

Option 2 is Add a remote SSE server. The page says the SSE transport is deprecated, so use HTTP where available. Claude Code tries HTTP first, and switches to SSE when the server doesn't accept it. That switch needs Claude Code v2.1.265 or later.

Option 3 is Add a local stdio server. The page says stdio servers run as local processes on your machine.

Here's the error to know. A JSON entry with a url but no type is a configuration error. Claude Code skips that server, and the message says to add type http.

The page also warns: Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection risk.

The page points to the Anthropic Directory for reviewed connectors. You can add any remote server listed there with claude mcp add.

The What you can do with MCP section lists Implement features from issue trackers. One quoted prompt reads: Create Gmail drafts inviting these 10 users to a feedback session. That's the page's example, not our test.

No terminal at all? Claude's Help Center has a page on Local MCP Servers on Claude Desktop. It says desktop extensions install local servers through single-click installable packages.

Go to Settings, Desktop app, and select Manage next to Extensions. Click Browse extensions, then click any Anthropic-reviewed tool. Click Install. Configure any required settings, like API keys.

The page says Desktop extensions support Node.js, Python, and binary MCP servers. Claude Desktop includes a built-in Node.js environment. The extension will automatically be available in your conversations.

To check a connection, click the plus button at the bottom of the chat box, then select Connectors.

If tools aren't available, the page says restart Claude Desktop. Then check the extension's configuration settings for missing required fields. If an install fails, the page says to re-download the file and verify disk space. On macOS, check System Preferences, Security and Privacy, if you receive security warnings.

When a developer marks a field sensitive, Claude Desktop encrypts it in the operating system's secure storage. That's Keychain on macOS and Credential Manager on Windows.

On Team and Enterprise plans, Owners and Primary Owners can enable or disable public desktop extensions. Enterprise policy controls at the user-machine level will override any in-app controls.

Back to the pricing page. Pro lists More usage than Free, every 5 hours and every week. It also lists Claude in Chrome and Microsoft 365. Its price line reads $20 if billed monthly, and mentions $200 billed up front with an annual discount.

The Max column lists 5x Pro usage every 5 hours and every week. It also lists $100 a month in API credits to build on the Claude Platform. The page also lists Priority access at high traffic times and Early access to advanced Claude features.

The footnote says usage limits apply. How fast you reach a limit depends on the model you use. It also names how long your chats are, and how large your files are. So your chats and files help decide the pace.

Two more lines matter. Price and plans are subject to change at Anthropic's discretion. Prices shown don't include applicable tax. The table's Billing cycle row reads Monthly and annual for Pro, and Monthly for Max.

For teams, the Team plan lists $25 per seat a month if billed monthly. It's for teams of 2 to 150. The feature table lists Admin controls for remote and local connectors under Team and Enterprise. The Model training row reads Opt-out on the individual plans.

The Best practices page says your first plain prompt in a fresh session usually already does the right thing. It also says conversations are compacted automatically before the context window fills. The page links four fixes. Tell Claude what it can't see. Give Claude a check to run. Then Enforce the rules that can't have exceptions, and Change a default.

It also includes A budget you need to stay under. Its table row How much it spends names --max-budget-usd with -p, and a spend limit you've set.

The page's table has two columns: Claude decides, and Claude Code enforces. It also says new terminal and VS Code sessions start in auto mode. That lets commands run without you approving each one. For rules that can't have exceptions, the page points to hooks and deny rules, not only CLAUDE.md.

Its test for what to write down: Could it find this by reading the code? If both answers are yes, leave it out.

So here's the answer. Free lists limited usage, chat, web search, files and code. Claude Code's own page says most surfaces need a subscription or Console account. The decision sits in the usage rows: Limited on Free, More on Pro, 5x Pro on Max. If you hit the Free limit often, Pro's More usage row is the next one to read.

Run claude --version, then claude mcp add, and the page's Notion example is yours to try. Then the copy-paste loop from the start has a documented replacement. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
